comparisons.peer_topic: Scope of Global Regulatory Compliance and Risks
comparisons.peer_summary: AMD's global operations are subject to a wide range of US and foreign laws, including those governing export control, data privacy, and AI. While current compliance has not materially impacted financial results, future regulatory changes or failure to comply could materially adversely affect capital expenditures, operations, competitive position, and expose the company to fines, sales limits, and reputational damage.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVIDIA and AMD disclose that US export control regulations significantly impact their ability to sell products in specific geographic regions, particularly China. However, the nature of the exposure differs: NVIDIA discloses specific, active licensing requirements imposed in FY2023 and FY2024 that explicitly restrict the export of its high-performance AI chips (A100, H100, etc.) to China and other restricted Country Groups (D1, D4, D5). AMD, by contrast, provides a generalized statement that while its operations are subject to export control laws, current compliance has not had a material adverse impact on its financial results or competitive position, without citing specific product bans or active licensing denials similar to NVIDIA's detailed operational constraints.

sentences.text: In October 2023, the USG announced new and updated licensing requirements that became effective in our fourth quarter of fiscal year 2024 for exports to China and Country Groups D1, D4, and D5 (including but not limited to Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Vietnam, but excluding Israel) of our products exceeding certain performance thresholds, including A100, A800, H100, H800, L4, L40, L40S and RTX 4090.

During the third quarter of fiscal year 2023, the U.S. government, or the USG, announced licensing requirements that, with certain exceptions, impact exports to China (including Hong Kong and Macau) and Russia of our A100 and H100 integrated circuits, DGX or any other systems or boards which incorporate A100 or H100 integrated circuits.

Our global operations are subject to various United States and foreign laws and regulations, including, but not limited to, those relating to export control, customs, intellectual property, data privacy and security, climate, environmental, health and safety requirements, cybersecurity, tax, employment, competition and anti-trust, anti-corruption, anti-bribery, conflict minerals, corporate governance, financial and other disclosures, and AI.
Compliance with these governmental laws and regulations do not presently have a material adverse impact on our capital expenditures, results of operations or competitive position.

sentences.text: This mismatch has resulted in both product shortages and excess inventory, has varied across our market platforms, and has significantly harmed our financial results.

Many additional factors have caused and/or could in the future cause us to either underestimate or overestimate our customers' future demand for our products, or otherwise cause a mismatch between supply and demand for our products and impact the timing and volume of our revenue, including:

We base our inventory levels in part on customers' estimates of demand for their products, which may not accurately predict the quantity or type of our products that our customers will want in the future or ultimately end up purchasing.

To the extent we fail to forecast demand and product mix accurately or are unable to increase production or secure sufficient capacity and there is a mismatch between supply and demand for our products, it could limit our ability to meet customer demand and have a material adverse effect on our business.

We may build inventories during periods of anticipated growth, and the cancellation or deferral of product orders or overproduction due to failure of anticipated orders to materialize could result in excess or obsolete inventory, which could result in write-downs of inventory and an adverse effect on gross margins.

In addition, we rely on third parties to provide certain information technology services to us, including help desk support, desktop application services, business and software support applications, server and storage administration, data center operations, database administration and voice, video and remote access.

Products as complex as those we offer may contain defects or failures when first introduced or when new versions or enhancements to existing products are released.

comparisons.peer_topic: Corporate Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting Obligations
comparisons.peer_summary: Evolving expectations and laws regarding corporate responsibility, including climate data reporting and third-party verification (e.g., in California), may impose additional compliance costs, require costly supply chain modifications, and result in reputational or financial harm if AMD fails to comply or meet stakeholder expectations.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVDA and AMD disclose that evolving stakeholder and regulatory scrutiny regarding corporate sustainability and responsibility practices creates risk of additional costs, reputational harm, and customer loss. NVDA specifically highlights risks related to shareholder, regulator, and customer dissatisfaction with sustainability goals, climate change, and human rights disclosures. Similarly, AMD identifies evolving expectations from governments, investors, and customers regarding corporate responsibility matters including environment, climate, energy, water, diversity, human rights, and cybersecurity, noting that failure to meet these expectations or comply with new laws could result in additional compliance costs and reputational harm. Both companies acknowledge the burden of monitoring, reporting, and complying with these evolving standards as a source of risk.

sentences.text: Increased scrutiny from shareholders, regulators and others regarding our corporate sustainability practices could result in additional costs or risks and adversely impact our reputation and willingness of customers and suppliers to do business with us.

Shareholder advocacy groups, certain investment funds, other market participants, shareholders, customers and government regulators have focused increasingly on corporate sustainability practices and disclosures, including those associated with climate change and human rights.

Evolving expectations from governments, investors, customers and other stakeholders regarding corporate responsibility matters could result in additional costs, harm to our reputation and a loss of customers.

There are evolving expectations from governments, investors, customers and other stakeholders regarding corporate responsibility matters including those involving the environment and climate, energy and water consumption, diversity and inclusion, human rights and cybersecurity.

comparisons.peer_topic: Risks related to responsible use of AI
comparisons.peer_summary: Issues related to the responsible use of AI may result in reputational, competitive, and financial harm and liability.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVIDIA and AMD disclose that the responsible use of AI technologies poses risks of reputational, financial, and competitive harm, as well as legal liability. NVIDIA explicitly links these risks to potential controversy over societal impact, copyright infringement, or human rights issues, whereas AMD’s disclosure is more general, stating broadly that such issues result in harm and liability. Both companies view the responsible use of AI as a significant risk factor affecting their business operations and reputation.

sentences.text: Issues relating to the responsible use of our technologies, including AI in our offerings, may result in reputational or financial harm and liability.

Concerns relating to the responsible use of new and evolving technologies, such as AI, in our products and services may result in reputational or financial harm and liability and may cause us to incur costs to resolve such issues.
◦Issues related to the responsible use of AI may result in reputational, competitive and financial harm and liability.

comparisons.peer_topic: AI Regulatory and Export Control Risks
comparisons.peer_summary: AMD faces significant risks from evolving AI regulations and export controls. U.S. BIS restrictions prevent shipping certain AMD Instinct ICs and Versal FPGAs to China and other sanctioned regions without licenses, and require NAC notifications, creating uncertainty around product roadmaps and market access. Additionally, evolving AI-specific laws like the EU AI Act and regulations on the responsible use of AI may impede the ability to offer certain products, increase compliance costs, create potential liability for third-party misuse or IP infringement, and raise complex intellectual property issues.
comparisons.comparison: This AMD disclosure covers responsible use of AI but significantly expands the scope to include specific regulatory and export control risks, such as U.S. BIS restrictions on shipments to China and the EU AI Act. While NVIDIA focuses on the ethical and societal consequences of AI adoption (e.g., unintended consequences, copyright), AMD highlights the tangible business impacts of regulatory compliance costs and potential product market access restrictions. Both acknowledge that legal and regulatory environments for AI are evolving and pose liability risks.

sentences.text: AI poses emerging legal, social, and ethical issues and presents risks and challenges that could affect its adoption, and therefore our business.

Our failure to adequately address concerns and regulations relating to the responsible use of AI by us or others could undermine public confidence in AI and slow adoption of AI in our products and services or cause reputational or financial harm.

We expect that the legal and regulatory environment relating to emerging technologies such as AI will continue to develop and could increase the cost of doing business, and create compliance risks and potential liability, all which may have a material adverse effect on our financial condition and results of operations.

As with many new emerging technologies, AI presents risks and challenges and increasing legal, social and ethical concerns relating to its responsible use that could affect the adoption of AI, and thus our business.

comparisons.peer_summary: AMD relies on patents, copyrights, and trade secrets to protect its technology but cannot assure adequate protection from infringement or misappropriation. Risks include patent applications failing to issue or being issued in disadvantageous forms, independent development of similar products by competitors, and difficulties in enforcing intellectual property rights in jurisdictions with weaker legal protections.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVIDIA and AMD disclose that reliance on patents, trademarks, copyrights, and trade secrets is critical for protecting their intellectual property, but both warn that this protection may be inadequate in foreign jurisdictions compared to the United States. NVIDIA specifically notes that 'Foreign laws may not protect our products or IP rights to the same extent as United States law,' while AMD states, 'In jurisdictions where foreign laws provide less intellectual property protection than afforded in the U.S. and abroad, our technology or other intellectual property may be compromised.' Additionally, both companies highlight the risk of competitors independently developing similar products or misappropriating confidential information. NVIDIA notes risks from employee hires by competitors and theft of trade secrets, while AMD notes that 'others may independently develop similar products' and that they cannot assure adequate protection from 'third-party infringement or from misappropriation.'

sentences.text: We rely on patents, trademarks, trade secrets, employee and third-party nondisclosure agreements, licensing arrangements and the laws of the countries in which we operate to protect our IP.
Foreign laws may not protect our products or IP rights to the same extent as United States law.

The theft or unauthorized use or publication of our trade secrets and other confidential information could harm our competitive position and reduce acceptance of our products; as a result, the value of our investment in research and development, product development and marketing could be reduced.
We also may face risks to our IP if our employees are hired by competitors.

We rely on a combination of protections provided by contracts, including confidentiality and nondisclosure agreements, copyrights, patents, trademarks and common law rights, such as trade secrets, to protect our intellectual property.

However, we cannot assure you that we will be able to adequately protect our technology or other intellectual property from third-party infringement or from misappropriation in the United States and abroad.
Despite our efforts to protect our intellectual property rights, others may independently develop similar products, duplicate our products or design around our patents and other rights.

In jurisdictions where foreign laws provide less intellectual property protection than afforded in the U.S. and abroad, our technology or other intellectual property may be compromised, and our business would be materially adversely affected.

It also maps to nvda_2024_1A_D044 which reiterates this general obligation and risk, adding specific reference to CCPA and AI concerns: 'We are subject to stringent and changing data privacy and security laws... comparisons.peer_summary: Strict privacy laws like GDPR and CCPA impose fines and penalties for data breaches, leading to ongoing costs for security enhancements, training, and remediation.
comparisons.comparison: Both Nvidia and AMD disclose that they are subject to strict, evolving data privacy laws like the GDPR and CCPA, and that non-compliance or concerns regarding data practices can lead to significant financial penalties, litigation, and reputational harm. However, Nvidia explicitly highlights the risk of reputational damage and adverse operating results stemming from consumer concerns about the use of their products for AI, whereas AMD focuses more on the direct financial burdens, citing ongoing and increasing costs for security enhancements, employee training, and remediation activities required to comply with these regulations.

sentences.text: We are subject to stringent and changing data privacy and security laws, rules, regulations and other obligations.

Concerns about our practices or the ultimate use of our products and services with regard to the collection, use, retention, security or disclosure of personal information or other privacy-related matters, including for use in AI, even if unfounded, could damage our reputation and adversely affect our operating results.

In addition, many governments have enacted and are continuing to enact strict privacy and security laws, such as the UK's and European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 (CCPA), as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act (CPRA), which provide for fines, penalties, and in the case of the CCPA and similar legislation, the basis for private claims for certain types of data breaches.

We anticipate ongoing and increasing costs related to enhancing and implementing information security controls, including costs related to upgrading application, computer, and network security components; training workers to maintain and monitor our security controls; investigating, responding to and remediating any data security breach, and addressing any related litigation or regulatory proceedings; mitigating reputational harm; and complying with external regulations.

Other jurisdictions have enacted or are considering similar cross-border personal data transfer laws and local personal data residency laws, any of which would increase the cost and complexity of doing business and could result in fines from regulators.

The inability to import personal data to the United States could significantly and negatively impact our business operations, limit our ability to collaborate with parties that are subject to European, China and other data privacy and security laws, or require us to increase our personal data processing capabilities in Europe and/or elsewhere at significant expense.

sentences.text: The net effect on our gross margin from inventory provisions and sales of items previously written down was an unfavorable impact of 2.7% in fiscal year 2024 and 7.5% in fiscal year 2023.

If in any period we anticipate a change in assumptions such as future demand or market conditions to be less favorable than our previous estimates, additional inventory write-downs may be required and would be reflected in cost of sales, resulting in a negative impact to our gross margin in that period.

If in any period we are able to sell inventories that had been written down to a level below the ultimate realized selling price in a previous period, related revenue would be recorded with a lower or no offsetting charge to cost of sales resulting in a net benefit to our gross margin in that period.

comparisons.peer_topic: Deferred tax asset valuation allowance policy
comparisons.peer_summary: A valuation allowance is recorded for deferred tax assets unless recovery is considered more-likely-than-not; conversely, if realization is deemed more-likely-than-not, existing valuation allowances may be reversed, resulting in a credit to income tax expense.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVDA and AMD disclose their policy for maintaining valuation allowances against deferred tax assets when realization is not considered more-likely-than-not. NVDA quantified its valuation allowance at $1.6 billion for fiscal 2024, citing jurisdictional projections of future taxable income as a key factor in determining assets not likely to be realized. AMD describes the qualitative framework, stating that a valuation allowance is recorded unless recovery is more-likely-than-not, without providing a specific aggregate dollar amount in this disclosure. Both companies agree that if realization becomes more-likely-than-not, they would reverse the allowance to recognize income tax benefits.

sentences.text: As of the end of fiscal years 2024 and 2023, we had a valuation allowance of $1.6 billion and $1.5 billion, respectively, related to capital loss carryforwards, and certain state and other deferred tax assets that management determined are not likely to be realized due, in part, to jurisdictional projections of future taxable income, including capital gains.
To the extent realization of the deferred tax assets becomes more-likely-than-not, we would recognize such deferred tax assets as income tax benefits during the period.

Unless recovery is considered more-likely-than-not (a probability level of more than 50%), we will record a charge to income tax expense in the form of a valuation allowance for the deferred tax assets that we estimate will not ultimately be recoverable or maintain the valuation allowance recorded in prior periods.

When considering all available evidence, if we determine it is more-likely-than-not we will realize our deferred tax assets, we will reverse some or all of the existing valuation allowance, which would result in a credit to income tax expense and the establishment of an asset in the period of reversal.

comparisons.peer_topic: Stock-based compensation valuation models and expense recognition policy
comparisons.peer_summary: The Company uses the Black-Scholes and Monte Carlo simulation models to estimate the fair value of stock options, RSUs, and ESPP shares at the grant date. Compensation expense is generally recognized using the straight-line method over the vesting period, with forfeitures estimated at grant and revised if necessary.
comparisons.comparison: Both NVIDIA and AMD disclose their methodologies for valuing stock-based compensation and recognizing expense for similar award types (RSUs, market-based PSUs, and ESPP). Both companies use the closing trading price (minus dividend discount) for standard RSUs and Black-Scholes for ESPP. NVIDIA uses Monte Carlo simulation for market-based PSUs, while AMD uses it for RSUs with market conditions; both apply straight-line expense recognition for these standard awards. A key difference is the recognition method for performance-based awards: NVIDIA uses an accelerated amortization model for corporate-target PSUs, whereas AMD recognizes expense for RSUs with performance or market conditions (PRSUs) ratably for each vesting tranche from the service inception date, rather than a generic accelerated model described in the summary.

sentences.text: We use the closing trading price of our common stock on the date of grant, minus a dividend yield discount, as the fair value of awards of restricted stock units, or RSUs, and performance stock units that are based on our corporate financial performance targets, or PSUs.
We use a Monte Carlo simulation on the date of grant to estimate the fair value of performance stock units that are based on market conditions, or market-based PSUs.

The compensation expense for RSUs and market-based PSUs is recognized using a straight-line attribution method over the requisite employee service period while compensation expense for PSUs is recognized using an accelerated amortization model.

We estimate the fair value of shares to be issued under our employee stock purchase plan, or ESPP, using the Black-Scholes model at the commencement of an offering period in March and September of each year.
Stock-based compensation for our ESPP is expensed using an accelerated amortization model.
The Company estimates stock-based compensation cost for stock options at the grant date based on the option's fair value as calculated by the Black-Scholes model.
For time-based restricted stock units (RSUs), fair value is based on the closing price of the Company's common stock on the grant date.
The Company estimates the grant-date fair value of RSUs that involve a market condition using the Monte Carlo simulation model.
The Company estimates the grant-date fair value of stock to be issued under the Company's Employee Stock Purchase plan (ESPP) using the Black-Scholes model.

Compensation expense is recognized over the vesting period of the applicable award using the straight-line method, except for the compensation expense related to RSUs with performance or market conditions (PRSUs), which are recognized ratably for each vesting tranche from the service inception date to the end of the requisite service period.
